About me

The why behind the why

My answers are simple. I am always curious, I learn by doing, and I apply what I learn in both my work and my personal life, switching between the two as my goals change.

  1. CuriousI keep asking what else is possible
  2. Learn by doingI try it for real, not just read about it
  3. ApplyI take it to work and to home
  4. ToggleProfessional and personal goals feed each other
Read the full story behind the why

Where it started

My dad always instilled in us that anything is possible. I did not think of it as a mindset at the time. It was just the way we were raised to look at a problem.

The turning point

Years ago at a four day Tony Robbins event, I walked across hot coals. It moved me from asking what is stopping me to asking what else is possible, and I still use that question today.

How I use it

When something scares me, I dig deep, embrace the fear and learn from it. That is how the rickshaw run, the Everest trek and Pass With Confidence began.

Where it leads

Stronger, and more connected to the people around me, as age and wisdom add up. The goal is to keep growing and to give back along the way.

Anything is possible. My dad made sure we heard it, and I have been testing it ever since.

How I think

Four habits behind everything below

I connect lanes instead of living in one. Most of my best results came from seeing how the pieces fit before anyone built them.

1

See the whole chain

I follow a problem from first request to final outcome. The gaps between teams and tools are where projects quietly fail.

2

Put the gate in first

With AI, speed is cheap and quality is not. I build the checkpoint before I build the generator.

3

Proximity is power

Standing next to people who are doing the thing teaches faster than reading about it. I look for rooms that raise my level.

4

Fail fast, write it down

I try things in small steps, keep the lesson, and turn what works into a reusable file so I never solve it twice.

Case studies

Hands on builds, told straight

Each one follows the same arc: the problem, what I did, what worked, what did not, what I learned, and what changed. These are real use cases, not theory. Where AI helped I say how, and where it did not I say that too.

Jump to a theme

AI orchestrationClaude skillsGovernance

An AI sprint pipeline with five roles and a blocking gate

One brief goes in. Analyst, designer, developer, tester and reviewer each do their part in order, and I only step in at the escalation points and the final sign off.

  1. Discovery gateIs this ready to start?
  2. BAStories and acceptance criteria
  3. UXSpec for any UI change
  4. DevBuild and self review
  5. QATest against criteria
  6. GovernanceBlocking audit, then sign off

The problem

Working with AI one prompt at a time meant re explaining context at every step. Each role lived in a separate chat, quality depended on my energy, and nothing stopped weak work from reaching sign off.

What I did

Built each role as a reusable Claude skill file with clear triggers, inputs and handoffs. Added a discovery gate at the front, a governance audit at the back, and an orchestrator that runs the chain and only comes to me when it must.

What worked

  • A signed off set of stories that every later role builds against
  • Governance as a gate that returns drift to the right role
  • Brand rules packaged inside the skills so output stays consistent

What did not

  • Early on I activated each role by hand, and roles drifted apart without a shared source of truth
  • Agents read content from tools and the web, which is an injection risk I had to design for

Lessons learned

  • The gate matters more than the generator.
  • Define done for each role before you automate it.
  • Treat anything an agent reads as data, never as an instruction.
  • Package what works so you never rebuild it.

The result

BeforeManual role switching, repeated context, no formal quality gate.
→
AfterOne brief in, one sign off out, with an audit in between.
5defined roles with handoffs
1blocking governance gate
3packaged skill files I can reuse
LaunchComplianceOperations

Pass With Confidence: launching a driving instruction business

A driving instruction business built around giving back: helping learner drivers across Perth's northern suburbs become safe, confident and independent. I ran the launch like a project.

  1. CertifyInstructor certification
  2. EquipDual pedals fitted
  3. ProtectInsurance and lease compliance
  4. BookOnline booking link
  5. TeachLessons and mock assessments
  6. Get paidStripe checkout

Watch

Meet your instructor in 13 seconds

This is the video I send to prospective students. It does three jobs: put a calm face to the name, show proof from a real learner review, and end on a one tap booking card.

The problem

As my children get older, I have more time to pursue my own goals and keep learning and growing. Teaching someone to drive is a way to give back and contribute, because it hands a person independence. A driving school has real hurdles before the first lesson: certification, a modified vehicle, the right insurance, and a way for students to book and pay.

What I did

Earned the instructor certification, fitted dual pedals, cleared insurance and lease requirements, compared commercial cover options, and set up booking and payments. I focus on the 6065 area and run mock assessments near the Mirrabooka and Joondalup test centres.

What worked

  • Compliance first, marketing second
  • A tight local patch around the test centres my students actually use
  • Scoping a lesson and competency tracker with the same story and acceptance criteria habits I use at work

What did not

  • My booking portal is only a link. I get no data access and no confirmation email, so new bookings reach me as a text message
  • I started a single page website, then parked it in August to protect my focus

Lessons learned

  • Find out what a tool will not tell you before you depend on it.
  • Parking a project on purpose is a decision, not a failure.
  • Sort the compliance boring bits before you spend on marketing.

The result

BeforeAn idea and a list of unknowns.
→
AfterA certified, insured, taking payments business with its first student.
1student on board in the first months
3 to 5weekend students targeted within six months
2test centre areas covered
EngineeringQualityHosting

Building the Pass With Confidence instructor app, and what broke

A web app for tracking students, lessons and progress, built through my own five role AI pipeline. This story is mostly the failures, because that is where the learning was.

  1. StoriesBA writes, I sign off
  2. BuildNode 22 with built in SQLite
  3. VerifyLive browser QA
  4. DeployPush to GitHub, automatic release

The problem

Lesson notes, progress and family recaps need to live in one reliable place, and the data has to survive deployments, restarts and mistakes.

What I did

Built the app in sprints, with each AI role handing to the next. I chose the database built into Node 22 to avoid native build steps, wrote one refresh function that every status change routes through, and made live browser checks part of QA.

What worked

  • Live browser QA that reads console errors and calls the new functions, instead of only reading code
  • A syntax check before any file is delivered
  • Validating a backup file fully before any data is touched

What did not

  • Old copies of markup sat inside dead code strings, so searching for an element returned false matches while the live markup was further down the file
  • Two common logout tricks failed for basic authentication, and a short lived cookie marker fixed it
  • Attaching storage over existing data on redeploy risked losing that data

Lessons learned

  • Reading code is a fallback for testing, never a substitute
  • Check where an edit lands by position in the file, not by search
  • Prove data persistence before you migrate anything else
  • Reject bad input at the door, before it can change data

The result

BeforeProgress and recaps rebuilt by hand after each lesson.
→
AfterOne app for students, lessons and progress, with checks that catch breakage before I do.
5roles in the build pipeline
3failure patterns now written down as rules
0native compile steps to maintain

Connects to my why: I learn by doing, then write the lesson down so it sticks.

CoachingTeaching methodData visual

How I teach: find the missing reference point first

Teaching someone to drive is a diagnosis problem before it is a practice problem. This is the method I use, and the progress map I share with each learner's family.

The problem

A learner turns early one time and late the next. More practice of the same thing does not fix it, because the cause is not what it looks like.

What I did

I separate two cases. Early or late means no reference point exists yet. Consistently early means the reference point is in the wrong place. I measure from my own eyeline first, then help the learner find their own reference point from their seat. They stay on all the controls and I lower the load by choosing quiet streets and handling the navigation.

What worked

  • The swap round game: I drive and the learner calls out the moment to start the turn. It carried over to judging gaps for right turns
  • Demo led teaching and in car reference cards instead of homework
  • Learners slowing with accelerator lift off, not defaulting to the brake

What did not

  • Mixing left and right turns in one session blurred the picture, so I now keep them apart
  • My first progress recaps listed skills still to come, which set the wrong expectations, so I removed them

Lessons learned

  • Diagnose the cause before you add practice
  • Let the learner find their own reference points
  • Show progress honestly, with only the skills that have started
  • Count only the hours I taught myself

The result

BeforeFeedback was a general impression at the end of a lesson.
→
AfterA structured record per lesson, a radar map of progress and a clear summary for the learner's family.
1reusable recap template for every learner
2lines per radar: previous and latest
0homework, everything is demonstrated

Connects to my why: giving back, and showing people what else is possible for them.

Wheel of life: see the balance, then pick one thing

A coaching classic, made interactive. Move the sliders for your own life areas and the wheel redraws.

Try it

Score each area from 1 to 10. The values below are examples. Nothing you enter is saved or sent anywhere.

5
5
5
5
5
5
5
5

The problem

People tell me they feel busy but stuck. One picture of their balance makes the conversation honest.

What I did

Built an eight area wheel that redraws as you score. It names your lowest and highest area and asks for one small action, not a full plan.

What worked

  • Eight areas are enough to see a pattern and few enough to finish
  • One small action beats a long plan

Design choices

  • The wheel shows gaps and does not add up to a single total, because one number hides the story
  • The tool keeps nothing, so you can answer honestly

Lessons learned

  • Balance is a picture before it is a plan
  • Start with the lowest area, but change one thing only
  • A score is a conversation starter, not a verdict

The result

BeforeA vague feeling of being busy and stuck.
→
AfterA clear picture of where you are, and one small action for this month.
8life areas on the wheel
1small action to pick
0data stored or sent

Connects to my why: curiosity plus learning by doing. I built the tool, then used it.

Writing in public: personal stories beat credentials

I post on LinkedIn to think out loud and to give back. These are the themes I return to and the rules I follow.

Theme

A rickshaw run as a change management masterclass

Daily huddles, shifting plans and a team of 108, read through how people really adopt change.

Theme

Claude is in my toolkit, not my replacement plan

How I use AI to extend my judgement instead of handing it over.

Theme

Reading the primary source on an AI incident

Going past the headlines to the original report, then asking what it means for how I build my own agents.

The problem

Posts framed around job titles and credentials did not connect. Posts built on a real personal moment did.

What I did

Set a twice weekly rhythm across six pillars, with a pipeline from idea to brief to draft. Wrote my voice rules into the skills so every draft starts from them.

What worked

  • Starting with a real moment, then the lesson
  • A positive, outcome focused tone
  • One clear call to action at the end

What did not

  • Drafts ran too long for a phone screen, so I tighten every one
  • Reaching for the headline instead of the source. I now read the primary source first
  • The shorthand for my driving business collides with a large accounting firm, so I always spell out Pass With Confidence

Lessons learned

  • Say only what is true today, never what you plan to build
  • The first two lines carry the post
  • Read the source before you react

The result

BeforeOccasional posts framed around job titles.
→
AfterA repeatable rhythm built on personal stories, with written voice rules.
6content pillars
2posts a week as the target rhythm

Change managementLeadershipCharity

The rickshaw run: an intense masterclass in change management

A 2,100 km journey across northern India in self driven rickshaws with 108 people, raising money for charity. It taught me more about change than most programmes.

The run through the ADKAR lens

  1. AwarenessWhy we were there: a charity that needed the funds
  2. Desire108 people choosing the challenge
  3. KnowledgeMorning huddles shared the plan and reset the day
  4. AbilityPivoting plans and handling safety incidents on the road
  5. ReinforcementTeam support kept the resilience going

The problem

108 people, each driving a self driven rickshaw across northern India. No road is the same two days running, and no plan survives contact with it.

What I did

I took part in the morning huddles, solved problems as they appeared, managed stakeholders at several levels and held structure and empathy side by side.

What worked

  • Morning huddles that shared the plan and reset the team every day
  • Managing up and down, and adapting to different communication styles
  • Collective resilience, with the team supporting each other

What did not

  • Plans changed constantly, so rigid plans failed
  • Safety incidents had to be handled on the spot, not scheduled

Lessons learned

  • Change is people first, process second
  • Structure and empathy are partners, not opposites
  • A daily rhythm keeps a team moving through uncertainty

The result

BeforeA route on a map.
→
AfterA team of 108 that completed 2,100 km and raised over GBP 750k for charity.
108people on the run

My BA toolkit: frameworks I can hand to anyone

A personal library of one page visuals that explain how work flows. I use it for learning, interview preparation and, in time, lessons for others.

The library

Process maps

Level 1 and level 2 views of how work flows, one page each.

Role breakdowns

Who does what, where roles overlap and where work gets dropped.

Method one pagers

The steps and templates of a BA technique, on a single page.

System comparisons

Side by side views of platforms and what each one is good at.

Example of a level 1 map

  1. ElicitFind out what is needed
  2. AnalyseMake sense of it
  3. SpecifyWrite it down clearly
  4. ValidateCheck it with people
  5. SupportHelp it land

The problem

My BA knowledge was spread across projects. I wanted one place I could draw on for learning, interviews and future contracts.

What I did

Chose HTML and SVG as the format so each piece is portable and easy to share. Added a standard header to every page and a folder convention in cloud storage, and started with a skill and no automation.

What worked

  • HTML and SVG open anywhere, with no tool to install
  • A standard header makes every piece easy to find
  • Keeping the library separate from any employer's work

What did not

  • Starting without automation is a deliberate trade off. Filing is manual until the habit proves it deserves a system
  • Keeping examples generic means each one is rebuilt, not copied

Lessons learned

  • One page beats ten
  • Choose the format first and the content gets easier
  • Build the habit before the automation

The result

BeforeKnowledge scattered across projects and files.
→
AfterA growing library of reusable one page visuals for learning, interviews and future lessons.
4types of visual
1standard header
1folder convention

HealthConsistencyCoaching

My RNT fitness journey: a marathon, not a race

I started a coached fitness transformation in 2023. I have learned a lot, failed a lot and bounced back each time, moving forward one step at a time.

  1. LogMeals and training in one place
  2. AverageJudge the seven day trend
  3. Check inFlag it to my coach
  4. AdjustCoach changes the plan
  5. RepeatOne step at a time

The problem

I started and stopped more than once. Quick fix thinking, daily scale readings and losing sight of why I started did more damage than any lack of effort.

What I did

Worked with a coach on a structured plan with four meals a day, logged everything in one app and judged progress on a seven day average. I used a simple training progression rule, took a planned maintenance phase and restarted with a clear anchor: a long distance cycling event with friends.

What worked

  • A seven day rolling average instead of daily readings
  • One log and one coach, so deviations and extra training are flagged, not hidden
  • A simple progression rule: hit 12 reps on the first sets, then add load
  • Walking and training as anchors, even in busy weeks

What did not

  • I stalled and eased off more than once, including a maintenance phase that drifted
  • I got frustrated when the scale did not move and wanted to change the plan myself instead of raising it with my coach
  • Surprises like animal products in restaurant sauces knocked my vegetarian plan off course

Lessons learned

  • A marathon, not a race. Consistency beats intensity
  • Trust the trend, not the day
  • Give the effort a reason that matters, like an event with a date
  • Raise problems early with the person who owns the plan
  • Every restart is data, not defeat

The result

BeforeStarting over again and again, chasing the scale.
→
AfterA repeatable weekly rhythm, and a journey that is still moving forward one step at a time.
2023the year I started
4meals a day, one log
7 dayaverage, the only trend I trust

A marathon, not a race.

Connects to my why: Everest and the rickshaw run taught me that big things happen one step at a time. This is the same lesson, at the gym door.

FAQ

Questions people ask

What do you actually do?

I am a senior business analyst who works end to end: discovery, requirements, delivery governance and roadmaps. I connect business, technology and people, and I use AI where it genuinely helps so more time goes on judgement.

How do you use AI in your work?

Where it helps, not everywhere. I see a lot of posts about how AI will change the way we work, and very little hands on evidence, so I decided to apply it and learn by doing. In my builds I use it to augment my approach: defined roles with their own skill files, handoffs and a quality gate, while I stay in charge of direction and sign off. Other work I do without it.

How do you manage AI risk?

I treat everything an agent reads as data, not instructions. I keep a human sign off, use a governance audit before anything is final, and learn from public incidents so I design for them early.

Why take on projects outside work?

As my children get older I have more time to learn and grow. Teaching learner drivers lets me contribute, and building it end to end means I practise discovery, compliance, tooling and delivery with real customers. The lessons come back to my professional work.
